newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Amnesty team in Tanzania over refugees' plight.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty team in Tanzania over refugees' plight.

text.p: A five-strong mission from the London-based human rights group Amnesty International arrived in Tanzania on Wednesday to urge the government not to force refugees back to war-torn and ethnically-divided Burundi.
The mission comes less than two weeks after Tanzania expelled 126 Burundian Hutu refugees, all of whom were killed by soldiers from the country's Tutsi-dominated army upon arrival home.
The Amnesty mission is led by Canada's former external affairs minister, Flora McDonald.

"The mission has come to Tanzania to urge the government to stop forcing refugees back to Burundi against their will as evidence mounts that hundreds of refugees returning from Tanzania have been massacred in recent weeks and months," Amnesty spokesman Marc Saghie told Reuters.
The human rights team is expected to talk with President Benjamin Mkapa and senior government officials.
Saghie expressed fears that Tanzania, traditionally a safe haven, may go ahead with more expulsions of Burundian refugees numbering more than 100,000.

The refugees fled a war in their tiny tea and coffee-growing central African nation between the Tutsi-dominated army and rebels from the majority Hutu tribe. Burundi's military, civil service and political life is controlled by the minority Tutsis.
The Amnesty team will also meet ambassadors from European countries, the United States envoy and heads of U.N. agencies.
Last month, Tanzania ordered more than 500,000 Rwandan refugees home.

UNHCR officials say well over 400,000 Rwandans returned to the land they fled after civil war and genocidal killings in 1994. U.N. human rights officials say more than 2,000 have since been arrested for their roles in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Burundi has been unstable since the 1993 murder of the country's first freely-elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu. A civil war between Hutu guerrillas and the Tutsi-dominated army has cost at least 150,000 lives.
Burundi's 25,000-strong army is overwhelmingly drawn from the Tutsi minority and has been blamed by human rights organisations for massacres of Hutus.

Some recent victims are former refugees, forced from camps in neighbouring eastern Zaire late last year by a rebellion. They returned to Burundi reluctantly and hundreds have been killed, relief workers say.
